name: Jamal Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Morning, Jamal, and thanks for fitting me in after your shift. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We've no links to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say stays private. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My day starts at three in the morning, so it's more like a night. I'm a junior buyer for Brandt's, a family-owned fruit and veg wholesaler at the city market, and we supply restaurants, schools and corner shops. I walk the stalls with a torch, check the tomatoes and the lettuces from the growers, and agree prices on the spot. Then by eight I'm back in the office on the phone ordering for tomorrow, which is the part I'm still slow at.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mr Brandt himself, Walter, he's sixty-four and he's been at that market since he was a boy. My dad was a porter there for thirty years, which is how I got the job. Walter says you buy with your hands and your nose, not with a computer, and I agree with him.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my fiancée Aisha, she works at the council housing office, and we're getting married next June. We've got about three months saved, but the wedding is eating into it. Family's a big deal for us, both sides, so it's not going to be a small wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: you can't smell a melon through a screen. Walter would say the same, louder. I don't post online, but at the market everyone would be nodding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but the market's got its own problems. The supermarkets buy straight from the big farms now, and our customers are mostly small places that are struggling. I'm not worried about AI, I'm worried about the corner shops closing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, learn the office ordering properly so I'm not the slow one. I'd ask Walter to let me deal with two of the growers on my own. And we'd keep the wedding on budget, no extras, so we don't come out of it with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose. Not about the machines, just about money and the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut from the wedding if you had to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second evening, probably, the one for the extended family. Aisha's mum would have words with me. But I'm not starting married life in debt, that's how my parents did it and it took them ten years to climb out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many corner shops have you lost as customers this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six, I think, since January. One was a man who'd bought from us for twenty years, he just retired and nobody took over. That kind of thing worries me more than any computer.

say: I'd say you can't **smell a melon** through a screen.
I'd agree with Walter, out loud at the **market**, rather than online.
think: The real threat is **supermarkets** buying direct and **corner shops** closing.
AI isn't my worry here; **money and the business** are.
do: Learn the **office ordering** properly so I'm not the slow one.
Ask Walter to let me handle **two growers** on my own.
Keep the **wedding on budget**, with no extras.
feel: **Uneasy** about money and the business, not about machines.
S0.quote: I'm not worried about AI, I'm worried about the corner shops closing.
fieldNote: His worry predates AI: **lost customers** and a squeezed family wholesaler.
He echoes Walter (the owner) on buying by **hand and nose**.
The **wedding cost** is a live pressure on his three months of savings.

steps.text: Learn Brandt's office ordering system properly
Ask Walter to hand him two growers of his own
Drop the second wedding evening if the budget slips

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, and that a business should keep its people if it can. But I'm not going to tell Walter how to run his firm. It's his name over the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the office part of my job goes. The ordering, the price sheets, the invoices, a computer does that. What's left is walking the market at three in the morning, and Walter's son already does half of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Walter straight what he's planning, man to man. If he's bringing in a system, I'd ask to be the one on the market floor, checking quality, since that's hands-on. And I'd look at whether the wedding could move to later in the year, so we keep more savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's not panic, but I'd be thinking about it every morning with the torch in my hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a business should keep its people. Would you expect help from the government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I'd rather the families and the firms sort it out. My uncle has a delivery business, he'd take me on if it came to it. That's how we do things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the new system, if Walter brought one in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to, I suppose, but I wouldn't be good at it. I can barely make the spreadsheet do what I want. I'd rather Walter kept me on the floor where I'm useful.

say: I'd say a business should **keep its people** if it can.
I wouldn't tell Walter how to run **his firm**, since his name is over the door.
think: The **office part** of my job, ordering and invoices, goes to a computer.
Walter's son already does half the **market walking**, which is what's left.
do: Ask Walter **man to man** what he's planning.
Ask to stay on the **market floor** checking quality, since it's hands-on.
Look at **moving the wedding** later to protect savings.
feel: **Anxious**, thinking about it every morning with the **torch** in hand.
S1.quote: What's left is walking the market at three in the morning, and Walter's son already does half of that.
fieldNote: He sees his job split into **office work** that goes and **floor work** that stays.
His **traditional view** looks to family and his uncle, not government.
He'd rather stay where he's useful than **learn the system** he expects to be bad at.

steps.text: Ask Walter to keep him on the market floor checking quality
Move the wedding later in the year to protect savings
Keep his uncle's delivery business as a fallback job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness, nobody asked for this. I'd say it at the market, at family dinners, everywhere. But I'd also say we look after our own, like we always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Brandt's either buys the system or goes under, because the big wholesalers will have it in a year. Either way the office half of my job is gone by 2028. The market floor lasts until about 2031, when robots can pick and check produce, so I'd have three years at best.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Aisha about a smaller wedding this June instead of next, so we're married and settled before it all hits. I'd ask my uncle about driving for his delivery business, because driving is hands-on too. We'd stop saving for a house and just keep cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be up at three anyway, but I'd be lying there before the alarm too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Aisha works at the council housing office. What about her job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Her job is forms and phone calls all day, so she's exposed same as me. My fiancée Aisha works in an office too, so both of us losing work at once is what frightens me most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say the market will always be there, because that's what he believes. I wouldn't argue with him. But I'd make sure he and Mum know we might need to stay with them a while.

say: I'd call it **madness** that nobody asked for, everywhere from market to dinner table.
I'd say we **look after our own**, like we always have.
think: Brandt's either **buys the system** or goes under within a year.
The **office half** goes by 2028; market work lasts until about **2031**.
do: Bring the **wedding forward** to a smaller one this June.
Ask my uncle about **driving** for his delivery business.
Stop saving for a house and **keep cash**.
feel: Most frightened that he and Aisha could **both lose work**.
S2.quote: My fiancée Aisha works in an office too, so both of us losing work at once is what frightens me most.
fieldNote: The **two-earner risk** drives his alarm, since Aisha (his fiancée) works in an office too.
He'd move the **wedding forward**, not back, to be settled before the shock.
He'd lean on **family**: his uncle's business and his parents' home.

steps.text: Hold a smaller wedding this June instead of next year
Ask his uncle for a driving job at the delivery business
Stop the house fund and keep savings as cash
Ask his parents whether he and Aisha could stay a while

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so let the businesses get on with it and let people like me get ready. I don't want the government stepping in and making a mess. Walter will work out what's best for Brandt's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the office side goes around 2031, but by then I'd hope to be properly good on the market floor. Robots checking lettuces around 2034 seems far off. Five years means the wedding goes ahead as planned, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year and see what the other wholesalers at the market actually do. Then I'd ask Walter to train me fully on the floor side, quality and grower deals. I'd keep the savings steady after the wedding, maybe rebuild to three months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, still. Not lying awake, but it's there in the background at the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait a year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people always say things are coming and half the time they don't. My dad heard the market was closing three times, so I'd want to see the change with my own eyes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Walter retires before 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it's his son's firm, and his son likes computers. That's the bit I'd worry about. I'd have to make myself useful to him, not just to Walter.

say: I'd say **five years** is fair warning; let businesses get on with it.
I'd say the **government** shouldn't step in and make a mess.
think: The **office side** goes around 2031, but I'd be strong on the market floor by then.
Five years means the **wedding** goes ahead as planned.
do: **Wait a year** to see what other market wholesalers do.
Ask Walter to train me fully on **quality and grower deals**.
Rebuild savings to **three months** after the wedding.
feel: **Anxious**, with the worry sitting in the background at the market.
S3.quote: My dad heard the market was closing three times, so I'd want to see the change with my own eyes first.
fieldNote: His **wait-and-see** comes from family memory of false alarms.
His real risk is **succession**: Walter's son likes computers.
He prefers **firms over government** making the call, matching his traditional view.

steps.text: Watch other market wholesalers for a year before acting
Ask Walter for full training in quality checks and grower deals
Rebuild savings to three months after the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, half the things people predict never happen. I'd say it with a smile. Walter would agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel all right. I'd be thirty-seven, married, probably with kids, and I'd hope to be running the floor at Brandt's. The robots in 2039 are a lifetime away for the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, learn the floor side and the growers properly, and keep the office side ticking over. After the wedding we'd start saving for a house again. I don't think I'd change much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, now and then. Mostly I'd put it out of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd have children by then. Would you tell them to go into the market?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children to learn a trade with their hands, like my dad told me. Plumbing, electrics, something people always need. Not an office job, not the way things are going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make this one worse for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Brandt's got bought out by one of the big chains. Then it doesn't matter how much warning there is, it's somebody else's decision. I'd want Walter to keep it in the family.

say: I'd say **ten years** is long, and half the predictions **never happen**.
I'd say it with a **smile**, and Walter would agree.
think: By 37 I'd hope to be **running the floor** at Brandt's.
**2039 robots** feel a lifetime away for the market.
do: **Carry on** learning the floor and grower side properly.
Keep the **office work** ticking over without pushing it.
feel: **Uneasy** now and then, mostly putting it out of mind.
S4.quote: I'd tell my children to learn a trade with their hands, like my dad told me.
fieldNote: With a decade, he feels **secure enough** to mostly ignore it.
His one fear is **Brandt's being bought** by a big chain.
He'd steer future children toward **trades**, echoing his dad.

steps.text: Keep learning the market floor and grower deals at Brandt's
Restart saving for a house after the wedding
Steer future children toward hands-on trades

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Aisha and I would both be in trouble at once, right as we're starting out. What would help is firms like Brandt's getting support to keep people on, and proper apprenticeships for trades. Not handouts, just a way to keep working.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the market itself. The city market has been there two hundred years, and people forget it's a community, not just a place to buy carrots. If it goes, a lot of families go with it.

headlineQuote: The city market has been there two hundred years, and people forget it's a community, not just a place to buy carrots.
portrait: Jamal is a **27-year-old junior buyer** at Brandt's, a family-owned fruit and veg wholesaler at the city market.
He starts at **3am**, trusts his hands and nose over screens, and never uses AI tools.
His **traditional view** looks to family, his employer and his uncle, not government help.
His sharpest fear is that he and Aisha, his fiancée in a council office, **both lose work** at once.
He'd **bring the wedding forward** in the fastest picture and wait and see in slower ones.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he and Aisha would both be in trouble at once.
whatWouldHelp: Support for firms to **keep people on**, and proper trade **apprenticeships**.
